quoted_clause: the factory made the wrong vendor claim cost nothing to the business
observed: The canary served 3,600 requests through the candidate, of which 12 had legal-subset failures. These were real user-facing failures (5% of production traffic was routed to the candidate). 'Cost nothing' overstates the outcome; the production impact was zero, but the canary impact was not.
correction: Change to 'cost the business no production traffic' or 'confined the cost to 12 canary requests' to match the stated arithmetic.
acceptance_test: The closing claim should be consistent with the failure count stated two sentences earlier.
verdict_evidence: ch21 L99 states 'the canary has served 3,600 requests with 12 legal-subset failures' and the same paragraph closes 'no user-visible regression … the factory made the wrong vendor claim cost nothing to the business' — 12 canary users received legal-subset failures, so 'cost nothing'/'no user-visible regression' overstates the outcome.
fix_instruction: Scope the claim: 'cost the business nothing in production traffic — the 12 legal-subset failures were confined to the canary'.

correction: Write 216,000/1,000 × $24.97 ≈ $5,394, or 216,000 × $24.97/1K without the extra ÷1,000. Apply the same fix to the $14.038/1K line.
acceptance_test: Recompute both lines from the displayed formula; the result must equal the printed dollar amount and carry dollar units.
verdict_evidence: The mini-case states the canary 'has served 3,600 requests with 12 legal-subset failures' (12/360 = 3.3% versus the incumbent's ~0.83%) and then closes 'No fire drill, no user-visible regression ... the factory made the wrong vendor claim cost nothing to the business' - 12 real requests got wrong answers.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the close to the bounded-blast-radius claim: '...bounded the wrong vendor claim to a ~3,600-request canary - 12 legal-subset requests answered wrongly - instead of 216,000 exposed requests', dropping 'no user-visible regression' and 'cost nothing'.

quoted_clause: No fire drill, no user-visible regression, no manual heroics — the factory made the wrong vendor claim cost nothing to the business
observed: The same mini-case reports 12 legal-subset failures among 3,600 canary requests. If the 5% canary is production traffic, those 12 are user-visible failures; the claim of zero user-visible regression and zero business cost contradicts the reported canary outcome.
correction: Say the regression was contained to the canary (12 users affected) and production-wide impact was avoided; or explicitly define the canary as shadow/internal traffic if zero user impact is intended.
acceptance_test: The mini-case either reports the 12 canary failures as user-visible but contained, or explicitly states the canary was shadow traffic; it does not claim zero user-visible impact while reporting failures.
verdict_evidence: chapter-21/chapter-21.md:99 says the canary 'has served 3,600 requests with 12 legal-subset failures' - a 5% production-traffic canary (:46) - then closes 'No fire drill, no user-visible regression, no manual heroics ... cost nothing to the business'. Twelve served requests were wrong answers to real users; the zero-impact claim contradicts the reported canary outcome.
fix_instruction: At chapter-21/chapter-21.md:99 say the regression was contained to the canary (~12 legal-subset requests affected) and production-wide exposure was avoided; or, if the canary is shadow/internal traffic, say so explicitly in :46 so zero user impact is true.

quoted_clause: Gate pass rate / false-promotion rate — how often a gated change later regresses in production; a rising value means the evaluation suite is losing fidelity.
observed: Gate pass rate and false-promotion rate are distinct. A rising gate pass rate can mean candidates are better or thresholds are looser; only a rising false-promotion rate directly indicates lost gate fidelity.
correction: Define them separately: gate pass rate measures candidate throughput; false-promotion rate measures gate fidelity. Only the latter's rise implies lost fidelity.
acceptance_test: The two metrics have separate definitions and the causal claim is attached only to false-promotion rate.
verdict_evidence: ch21 l.46-48: subsection headed '**Cost of a good gated release.**' gives only '~3,600 requests' and no dollar figure, while the ungated side carries $5,394 (216,000 x $24.97/1K); 3,600 x $24.97/1K ~ $90 is never stated.
fix_instruction: Either retitle that subsection 'Exposure of a gated release' or add the missing cost line ('serving cost of the ~3,600 canary requests ~ 3,600 x $24.97/1K ~ $90, against the ungated path's $5,394'); do not add unquantified duplicated-residency claims.

correction: Rename the calculation 'baseline serving cost of the exposed requests' and separately state the incremental business cost is unquantified; or compute only incremental cost.

page_hint: Ch 21 §8 mini-case, sentence introducing the 240 ms figure
quoted_clause: The candidate improves quality on the main subset but adds 240 ms to p95 TTFT; the canary has served 3,600 requests with 12 legal-subset failures
observed: The 240 ms TTFT regression is introduced and then never used. On the canonical numbers it independently breaches the SLO: 1.9 s + 0.24 s = 2.14 s > the 2 s p95 TTFT SLO. The mini-case attributes the gate firing solely to the quality regression, leaving a second, independent firing condition unexamined - which weakens the lesson that the gate must include deployment metrics (a point the chapter's own Common Mistakes section makes).
correction: Add one sentence: 'The candidate also breaches the 2 s p95 TTFT SLO on its own (1.9 s + 240 ms = 2.14 s), so the gate would have fired on the deployment metric even without the legal-subset quality regression - which is exactly why the gate must score quality and serving together.'
acceptance_test: Every numeric regression introduced in the mini-case is either used in the reasoning or explicitly set aside; the 240 ms figure is either analyzed or removed.
verdict_evidence: ch21 l.99 introduces '+240 ms to p95 TTFT' and never uses it; 1.9 s + 0.24 s = 2.14 s > the 2 s p95 SLO, so the candidate breaches on serving alone while the narrative attributes the firing to quality, and l.73 says the gate must include deployment metrics.
fix_instruction: Add one sentence to the ch21 §8 mini-case: 'The candidate also breaches the 2 s p95 TTFT SLO on its own (1.9 s + 240 ms = 2.14 s), so the gate would have fired on the serving metric even without the legal-subset regression.'
